doc.title: Tony Parenti and Anthony Sbarbaro Interview, 1959-06-29

chapter: New Orleans dance halls and cabarets
title: Parenti's self-intro; first jazz dance at the Lusitania; the Black Cat
summary: Parenti introduces himself, recalls his first jazz dance upstairs at the Lusitania hall with Eddie Edwards and a gunshot scare, then both Tonys trade memories of pay, the Black Cat, Tom Anderson and Sophie Tucker.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: My name is Tony Perinti. Without a question of being a New Orleans little fellow that has still carried on up to the moment with the appreciation of our New Orleans basic background and jazz. However, being a little individual, I had to do many other types of playing. For example, having the original foundation from our very early childhood days and taking lessons and studying music, I have also been a part of the so-called legitimate field and also the commercial value of things. But at the moment, I have finally resigned myself down to working and playing only jazz. No conductors to follow, no music to read, and no metal strains. So now all I do is call out the tune, what key, knock off two beats and live forever. And it's exactly what I'm doing right now. But Tony Spargo, who's sitting right opposite me right now, and incidentally this is a very warm day. I'm drinking a can of cold beer and I just... It's about 96 out, I'll tell you that much. It is 96 out, Tony. No, it's after, it's over 90, I'll tell you that. Well, that's a little warmer than the days in our early New Orleans career. It used to get hot down there, but not any much hotter than it is right now. Yeah, but then you had Millenburg where you could cool off. You can't cool off up here. Well, Millenburg is the place where you not only can cool off, but you can also get feeling pretty good while you're cooling off. Hey, Tony, let me ask you a question. As long as we reminisce a little bit, I can recall, vaguely, when I just started to play a little jazz, when I think Eddie Edwards asked me to come up to some little place on the Leeson field upstairs. They had a dance, and of course, that was during the time when the town was wide open, which meant that I had never seen anything like that, but in as much that Eddie had happened to pass on Dolphine, and St. Anne Street, where my father had the shoemaker shop, and hearing me practice from the street, and the fact that Eddie asked my dad who was playing clarinet, and my dad said, that's my boy, that's my boy, Tony, which means that I came out and I met Eddie Edwards, who in turn asked me to come up to this dance hall on Leeson field upstairs, and I don't remember the name of it. Lusitania. Lusitania. Lusitania, all right. Still there. Still there. I went up there, that for my first value, and I'm still in my short pants. The object in view is the reason why I wanted to ask you was to find out the name of that place, and I'm glad you were there. Every time I visit New Orleans, and I just recently got back there from a trip, I always go look at that building as an old remembrance. It's still there, broken down, all dilapidated. They all lose the town. My gracious alab. I've never seen that place. The next time I go down home. Fahey Hagen used to own it at that time. I want to go up there and take a peek at that. And incidentally, as long as I brought that up, it was very quaint, and the fact that I went up there with my clarinet, there was my recollections, I hope I'm right, but I vaguely remember, that it was a boy named Lane, Patsy Lane. Pansy. Pansy Lane, who played drums. He had a gold tooth in his mouth. Exactly. And the trumpet player was named Manuel Blessing or something like that. Manuel Mello. Blessing. Blessing. Well, it was a blessing. Blessing. Something like that. It was a Manuel Blessing, Manuel Mello. Well, the blessing is the boy that I remember, who was an awfully nice fellow. I can't remember the clarinet player because the only reason why I was asked to come up there was to listen and sit in, not to work. It was a matter of me wanting to know how I could do. I think everybody else got started. So, I went up there and I never saw anything like that in my life before because there were kind of, a lot of fights in this thing. I used to get a big price playing those dances up there, $1.25. Yeah. Well, whatever it was, the thing that fascinated me was that I had afterwards found out that all the girls that were working in the red light district were there with their so-called boyfriends. And that was the element of the people that patronized the dance hall. Dance hall, yeah. And our jazz, as I found out much later, was only accepted in that type of dance because I know society had not accepted our type of jazz at that time. Not yet, no. And so I did sit in and play and it was very, very interesting and everybody was very complimentary to me and flattering until, of course, a certain thing happened. There was a, there was shooting, a gunshot. Yeah. And I, I got scared, so scared that I hit behind a base drum like as if that's the big saving situation. Those days you could carry a gun without worrying about the cops. There was nothing about the stuff, you know. And we had intermission. We used to go in the back room to smoke a little happy cigarettes and things like that. And there was, two of the boys that I, I mentioned had their so-called girlfriends who also worked back in the red light district. So the whole format was quite interesting because that was the, my very beginning in the so-called New Orleans jazz. But where were you then, Tony? Well, I was either working for the sewage and water board and then playing clubbing, which you might call what we call clubbing up there. Yeah. But I remember that, uh, Lusitania because we used to do two nights a week there and that was a lot of money for us to make a dollar and a quarter a night. Yeah. Tony, you know, it often comes to me and I, I feel that I would like to live back in those days with a dollar and a quarter than to live today with a hundred and a quarter. So because somehow or another, the dollar quarter was a big deal. Like, uh, uh, uh, you could walk with that dollar. Dollar was about four times the size of the one we got now. Anyhow. Well, I sold watermelons two for a nickel in those days. Well, what? Two for a two for a watermelons, two for a nickel. But I mean, I'd like to say that it's a wonderful thing to go back, but I don't think in those days you could make, put any money because I think my top salary after I well got recognized from 10.50 a week, they finally gave me $14 a week to work in a black hat. That was the number two spot alongside of Tom Anderson. I remember that. See? And that was a big salary to give for $14 a week. Oh my God, that's my father. He was only making about $15 a week. You know? I remember that. And he wanted me to pull out of there because I had short pants on. And the fellow owned the place. Uh, I won't tell you his name because, but, uh, he was a sheriff, you know, and he come over there. Well, what year was that in, Tony? Because I worked at the hay market myself. It was anyway after 12, 1912, 13, 14, because 15, I had already been out in Millenburg. Is that right? It had to be in, it had to be in 1914 when the, the boat went down, I was playing those places. Lucitania. Lucitania went down. That's right. That's when I was working. Well, the reason why I mentioned that is because you were bringing me back. Every year, whenever that boat went down, that's when I was working in there and I was, in other words, I was on my way. I had gotten away from what I call the spasm bands. What, uh, we used to call them, uh, spasm bands. That's right. My band. That's right. You know? I was going to play for a keg of beer. I would go down to somebody's house and play a party for a keg of beer. But, uh, whatever day that, uh, boat, you know, Lusitania, that year, I was working in the black cat. That's something that will stick in my mind, you know? You know, it does. In fact, it sticks in my mind that you bringing me back to that particular time. I don't know if you remember a little fiddle player named Johnny Kuroge. No, I don't. Well, uh. I remember Fink in those days. Huh? Max Fink was the only one. Oh, well, that was much later. Much later. Yeah. Much later. Max Fink is the guy that I took his place at the Liberty Theater. That's right. He got in trouble with the... But he was, uh, he was the king and the pharaohs and something like that. But there was a little boy named Johnny Kuroge, who, uh, was around my age, but very talented. And I'm trying to remember what year it was, but Johnny got the job at the, uh, what do you call it? The Haymarket right near, on Ramport Street near Canal. What's the name of that big, uh, it was a pretty good little nightclub. The Ramport near Canal. Yeah. North Ramport. North Ramport now. Yeah. North Ramport. North Ramport was. Between Canal and the street below. Between, between, between Canal and the street below. More George Canal Street. It was, uh. I was in there. It was a Black Cat. And there was a Tom Anderson. That's the one. Tom Anderson. That's the name. Tom Anderson. That's the name. Now that you've brought it up. That was the one. That was the one. Overall. That was, uh, a place that we played there. Wasn't, didn't play very long. I played there a month, I think, or something. Because during that time, that was the first time I had ever, ever seen Sophie Tucker. I didn't remember Sophie Tucker down there. Well, no. But I mean, she was at one of those theaters. Oh, sure. She was at a A-Day. Yeah. And we played, uh, somebody said, here's Sophie Tucker coming in. So we went into our best little, uh, jazz tune was Tiger Rag. So we were rambling, we were rambling on Tiger Rag. And then after that, it was mentioned that, uh, to give her announcement, which we did, and she got up and took a bow and then came up and sang. Song which was called the Black Cat, about the number two place. Because we used to look forward to finishing the night, 9 to 5 in the morning, for $1.50 a night. Then when I wanted to leave, they'd finally come across and give me $2 a night, seven days a week, no six or five. But Tom Anderson, and here's something that'll stick in my memory. I'll never forget this fellow. It was always trios, you know, they never had any big fans. They had them over the track, but never in the cabarets. That's right. This fellow would read the racing form. We had every bit of 12 girls. You know, no girls came in that place. The girls were working there. Men just came in there. He would read the racing form all night long, and with those girls sitting at that table, hoarse, or a little tight, or a little tired, or whatever, and they're changing keys every minute on them, that fellow would read that racing form and play for those girls all night long and whatever key they wanted. I'll never forget it. You don't remember his name? Art something. I can't get his license. He was either a Spanish boy or a Mexican boy or something. Because you're reminding me the days when I played at the Pop Cabaret, where we had a piano player named Roy Barton. Yeah. Now, this Roy Barton was a very handsome-looking fellow, and he did the same thing. He put these girls up in their right turns to sing, and with the right tunes and the right keys, and also because of the fact, like you say, Yeah, keep changing. The throat is not too good. Lure, yeah. He'd drop a tone automatically for the next chorus, and the girl would go into it. Things like that. This is a remarkable feat, because it's so helped me. God, this fellow never did anything. God된 stuff with stuff
